# The Commissar's Confession

---

## I. The List

Seven names and the ink not yet dry, the ink still catching light when I tilted the paper toward the window, and I thought: *the ink is the same*. The same iron gall, the same lampblack suspension that Citizeness Desforges mixed in the back of the print shop on Rue Saint-Jacques where the press had not run in fourteen months but where the smell of it—that ferric, almost blood-taste smell of fresh ink on wet paper—still lived in the walls, in the grain of the wood, in the skin of her hands when she passed me the folded broadsheets that I tucked inside my coat lining, against my ribs, where they crinkled when I breathed and I'd walk through the Tuileries gardens breathing shallowly so the paper wouldn't sound, so the paper wouldn't betray me to the men I was already betraying.

Seven names. I counted them again.

The first: Desforges, Marie-Anne, née Cloutier. Widow. Printer. Age forty-three. *Suspected of distributing seditious materials in contravention of the Law of 22 Prairial.*

The Law of 22 Prairial which I had helped draft. Which I had sat in the green room of the Committee and sharpened with my suggestions, my careful amendments, my—what had Couthon called it—my *admirable precision*. Citizen Inspector Maillard understands the machinery of justice, Couthon had said, and Saint-Just had looked at me with those marble-still eyes, those eyes that never moved independently of his head as though his entire skull were a single fixed instrument of appraisal, and he'd said nothing, which was worse.

The seventh name does not matter yet. I will come to the seventh.

Robespierre's hand on my shoulder. How small his hands were. How carefully manicured, the nails filed to uniform crescents, and the slight tremor in the fingers that everyone saw and no one mentioned, the way one does not mention the smell in a room where someone is dying—

"Maillard, this matter requires your personal attention."

"Citizen, I—"

"Your *personal* attention. The Committee has observed that certain networks persist. That the hydra regenerates its heads. We require not merely the blade but the cauterization. You understand. You have always understood."

And I had. God help me, that was the truest thing the Incorruptible ever said about me. I understood. I had always understood. That was precisely the problem.

---

## II. Three Years

Begin at the beginning. No—there is no beginning. There is only the middle, the endless grinding middle of it, the revolution eating itself like the serpent and I inside the coils, moving with the contractions, peristalsis of history and I the undigested thing working my way through.

*June 1791.* The King's flight to Varennes, and Paris drunk on betrayal, and I was twenty-six years old and believed that the word *republic* was a spell that could transmute the lead of human nature into something bright and untarnishable. I believed this. I need you to understand that I believed this with the whole of my body, the way a man believes in the floor beneath his feet—not as proposition but as condition, as the given ground of everything. Inspector of the second municipal district. A small man with a small jurisdiction and a burning unshakeable conviction that the people, once freed from the grotesque machinery of monarchy, would govern themselves with the rational decency that God or Nature had encoded in their—

Enough. I cannot even write the words without hearing how Citizeness Desforges would have laughed. That low, dry laugh, more exhalation than sound. *You are very young, Citizen Inspector. The people are not an abstraction. The people are Madame Fournier on the third floor who waters her milk and beats her daughter. The people are the tanner on Rue Mouffetard who cheats on weights. The people are you and I, sitting in this room, deciding what to print, which means deciding what to hide, which means we are already tyrants on the smallest possible scale. The only question is whether we are honest about it.*

The network. Say the word. Goupil recruited me—Goupil with his bad teeth and his Montesquieu and his dangerous, infectious certainty that the revolution could be saved from itself if only the right information reached the right hands at the right moment. *We need someone inside, Maillard. Inside the apparatus. The Committee is consolidating. Hébert's people are pushing for more blood, always more blood, and the Dantonists are trying to brake the wheel but they're being outmaneuvered and we need eyes in the room where the warrants are signed.*

I said yes.

I said yes because I still believed, then, that there was a meaningful difference between the revolution I'd imagined and the revolution that was happening. That the gap could be closed. That a man positioned at the right joint of the machine could apply pressure—not much, just enough—to deflect the blade by the few degrees necessary to miss the neck of someone who did not deserve to die.

And for a time it worked. For a time I was brilliant at it. I will not pretend to a false modesty: I was *brilliant*. I knew which denunciations to accelerate and which to mire in procedural delay. I knew which clerks could be trusted with a misfiled document, which guards would look away for thirty seconds at the Conciergerie gate when a prisoner needed to pass a message. I developed a sense for the rhythm of the Committee's attention—the way suspicion moved through that body like weather, like a pressure system, now pressing down on the Girondins, now swinging toward the enragés, and in the calm eye of each rotation there was space, a few days, sometimes a few hours, in which a name could be struck from a list or a family warned or a passport arranged.

Seventeen people. I keep the count the way a miser keeps his coins, fingering each one in the dark. Seventeen people who are alive because I was inside the machine and knew which lever to pull.

Does it matter? Does seventeen matter against the thousands? The mathematics of it—and this is what hollows me, this is the calculation that wakes me at four in the morning in the narrow bed in my apartment on Rue de la Ferronnerie, where the sheets smell of sweat and the walls are thin enough to hear my neighbor weeping—the mathematics of it is that for every name I struck from a list, I had to leave three others. Four others. Ten. To remove too many would have been noticed. Would have been the anomaly that drew Saint-Just's fixed and turning head toward me. So I chose. I calculated. I weighed one life against another on the scales of probability and strategic value and—I will say it—personal attachment, though I tried not to, though I swore to myself that I was rational about it, dispassionate, that I selected for maximum impact and network preservation and not because this woman had a daughter the age of my dead sister or because that man had once, in a café, said something so piercingly true about the nature of freedom that I carried it in my chest for weeks like a shard of glass.

I chose. And the ones I did not choose went to the Place de la Révolution and the blade came down and the crowd cheered or didn't and the tumbril was loaded again and I was inside the machine and the machine was inside me and we were becoming, the machine and I, indistinguishable.

---

## III. The Printer's Widow

Marie-Anne Desforges. I must write about her directly or I will circle forever.

Her husband, Jean-Claude, had printed pamphlets for the Cordeliers in the early days—the real early days, before the Cordeliers became Hébert's instrument, when the club still carried some residual heat from Danton's first idealism. Jean-Claude died in September 1792—not the massacres, the dysentery, the ordinary bloody flux that kills more revolutionaries than any guillotine, and Marie-Anne kept the shop, kept the press, kept the network of distribution that her husband had built through the labyrinth of streets between the Panthéon and the river.

Goupil brought me to her in March of 1793. The shop was cold, I remember that. The press stood like a skeleton of iron and wood in the back room and the windows were filmed with condensation and she was setting type. Still setting type. Her fingers moving over the case with that unconscious precision, pulling letters without looking, composing right-to-left and inverted so that the words emerged mirror-reversed from her hands and only became legible when committed to paper, when pressed into existence—

I am delaying again.

She looked at me and said: "So you are the one inside."

"Yes."

"And what have you learned, being inside?"

I told her what I knew. The Committee's plans for the Law of Suspects. The expanding definition of *enemy of the people*. The way the machinery of denunciation was being streamlined, regularized, made efficient—made, I said, *industrial*.

She listened without interrupting. Then she said something I have turned over in my mind every day since, something I return to the way the tongue returns to the broken tooth, compulsively, knowing it will hurt:

"You speak of the machine as though you are not part of it. But you are. Every day you sit in that room, you give it legitimacy. Every warrant you *don't* sabotage is a warrant you've signed. You understand this? The question is not whether your hands are clean. They are not. They cannot be. The question is only what you are purchasing with the dirt on them, and whether the price is honest."

The price. Seventeen lives. Against my complicity in—how many? I stopped counting after Thermidor. I could not bear to count.

She taught me many things, Marie-Anne Desforges. She taught me that the broadsheets we produced—the carefully worded arguments for clemency, for legal process, for the distinction between justice and vengeance—were not weapons but seed. *We are not fighting this revolution*, she said. *We are writing to the next one. To the people who will come after and try to understand what happened here and who will need to know that not everyone was drunk on blood, that some people saw clearly and said so and were killed for it but said so anyway.* She taught me to set type. She taught me that the compositor's art is the art of reversal—you must think backward to produce something that reads forward, you must hold the mirror-image in your mind and trust that the impression, the final pressing of ink into paper, will rectify what your hands have made alien.

She also taught me—but this is private, and the revolution has taken everything else, and I will keep this, I will hold it inside where the broadsheets used to crinkle against my ribs, I will keep the specific quality of lamplight on the side of her face when she looked up from the press with ink on her fingers and her mouth slightly open as though about to speak and then not speaking, just looking, just—

I will keep that.

---

## IV. Walking

*Germinal, Year II. The morning of the 14th.*

The tumbrils are late. A wheel has broken on the Pont au Change and the first cart is delayed and I am standing in the courtyard of the Conciergerie with the list in my hand and the seven names on the list and the seven bodies attached to the names standing or sitting or crouching against the wall in the grey early light and Marie-Anne is the third from the left, her hands bound in front of her, her hair cut short—they cut the hair, in the cell, before transport, a practicality, so the blade has a clean path to the neck—and she is looking at me.

She is looking at me and her face is—

What is her face? I must be precise. I owe her precision, at least, since I can give her nothing else. Her face is not surprised. That is the first thing. She knew. She must have known, when they took her, that the inside man had either been turned or been overruled, that the network had been pierced from above by a force greater than my small deflections could counter. Her face is not accusatory. This is worse. Accusation I could metabolize, could fold into the structure of guilt I carry like a cathedral's weight on its flying buttresses—an external pressure that the architecture converts into stability. But she is not accusing me. She is *reading* me. The way she read proof sheets. Scanning for errors, for misalignments, for the letter that has slipped and will print as a meaningless smudge unless corrected before the press comes down.

And I think: *she is looking for the man she knew*.

And I think: *she will not find him*.

The courtyard. The sounds. I should describe the sounds because they are what remain when I close my eyes, when I try to reconstruct the morning in the ordered sequence that consciousness, in its shattering, refused to maintain. The sound of boots on wet cobblestones—the guards, four of them, National Guard detachment, two of them boys who cannot be older than nineteen with faces the color of rendering fat. The sound of iron on iron—the gate mechanism, the manacle chains, the bolt of the tumbril's tailgate. The sound of breathing, which is to say the sound of seven people who are about to die and who know it and whose bodies are performing the animal work of continuing to breathe, to oxygenate blood that will, within the hour, be draining between the cobblestones of the Place de la Révolution, and this biological optimism, this cellular refusal to accept what the mind has already understood—

I cannot bear it.

But I must bear it. That is the specific cruelty of my position: I must bear it while appearing to orchestrate it, while holding the list and checking the names and verifying that the right persons have been loaded in the right order and that the procession will follow the correct route—Rue de la Barillerie to the Pont Neuf, across to the Right Bank, along the quai to the Place—and that the executioner's apparatus has been inspected and the blade has been sharpened and the drainage channel has been flushed since yesterday's use—

These details. I know these details because I have overseen this process before. Eleven times. Fifty-three people, prior to today. I know the procedure the way I know my own name, which is to say: automatically, without reflection, the knowledge embedded in the body rather than the mind so that my hands perform the inspection and my voice performs the commands and my legs carry me alongside the tumbril while elsewhere, above, in the attic of my skull, a different man is screaming.

Goupil is dead. I should say this now because it will explain the calculation I am performing even as I walk, even as my boots find the cobblestones and my hand grips the list and my mouth forms the words *avancez, avancez*. Goupil has been dead for six weeks. His body is in the mass grave at Picpus, or what remains of his body—I do not know the rate of decomposition, I do not want to know it, but the image insists, Goupil's bad teeth in the earth, Goupil's Montesquieu rotting with him, the annotated copy he carried everywhere with the margins full of tiny handwriting that leaned forward as though the words themselves were in a hurry—

Goupil was taken on a denunciation. A neighbor. A man whose name I learned afterward and filed in the precise, cold archive of my memory where I keep the names of everyone who has murdered by paperwork, by whisper, by the raising of a hand at a section meeting to say *I have something to report about the citizen on the fourth floor*.
